turns.text:
My husband won't even look at a job offer I worked hard for, and I have to answer by Friday. I've been passed over for promotion twice in two years. In April I told him I felt stuck and wanted to look at jobs, including outside Pittsburgh. I sent him a few postings and he said, "Can we not do this every few days? Tell me when something's real."

So I did. I applied for a design lead role in Denver, got through the interviews and the final round, and the night the offer came I told him everything. It's $148,000, up from $112,000. I wasn't going to start a fight over a job I didn't have.

He said it sounded like I'd already decided, left the table, and slept in the guest room. I told him I hadn't decided anything and wanted us to decide together. I forwarded him the offer letter and he hasn't opened it. Every time I bring it up he says he won't talk about it until I explain why I hid it. He's punishing me for doing exactly what he asked. I think he'd rather I stay stuck than have anything change.

I'm hurt and honestly kind of furious. Am I wrong to want him to actually look at the offer before Friday?

You are absolutely not wrong to want him to look at the offer. You achieved something massive—a huge salary bump, a senior title, and a major breakthrough after two painful years of being passed over—and instead of celebrating with you, your partner is shutting you out while a strict Friday deadline ticks down. Your frustration and anger are entirely justified.

What you are experiencing right now is a painful collision between literal communication and emotional expectations. When he originally said, "Tell me when something's real," you took that as a directive to shield him from the day-to-day anxiety of the job hunt until you had a tangible offer in hand. You were trying to respect his boundary. However, a cross-country move to Denver is a massive life shift. To him, the prospect of moving likely only felt "real" if he was part of the escalating reality of the interview process. Presenting a finalized offer for a job in another state understandably felt to him less like an invitation to decide together and more like a finalized plan he was just being informed about.

Understanding why he feels blindsided does not excuse his current behavior. **Stonewalling you, sleeping in the guest room, and refusing to open the letter is deeply unfair and unproductive.** He is making this entirely about his bruised ego rather than the very real, time-sensitive life decision sitting in front of both of you. You cannot put a corporate Friday deadline on hold while he punishes you for a miscommunication.

To break this stalemate before Friday, you may need to address his grievance directly so you can force a pivot to the actual decision. You might try confronting the tension head-on by saying something like: **"I did not hide this to leave you out. I took your words literally because I didn’t want to cause unnecessary stress until the job was a reality. I see now that keeping the interview process to myself made you feel blindsided, and for that, I apologize. But I have not made a decision. I want us to decide together, and I need my partner to look at this with me right now because Friday is not moving."**

By naming the miscommunication and validating his feeling of being surprised, you remove his main excuse to keep stalling. You are addressing the "why you hid it" prerequisite he set, clearing the path to talk about the job. If he still refuses to look at the offer after you extend that olive branch, you have a much larger problem to confront—because it would confirm your fear that he would rather you stay stuck than deal with change.

If Thursday night arrives and he is still refusing to open that letter, are you prepared to make the choice about taking the Denver job on your own?

You are completely justified in feeling furious, and you are entirely right that holding a strict Friday deadline hostage is an unfair, punitive way for him to handle his feelings.

However, approaching this as a strict binary of who is "right" and who is "wrong" is likely going to keep you trapped in this standoff. You are factually right because you followed his literal instructions to wait until things were real. But emotionally, **winning the argument about who followed the rules better will not resolve the tension or get him to open that letter.**

He is reacting from a place of shock and insecurity. To him, the leap from "I want to look at jobs outside Pittsburgh" to "I have a finalized offer in Denver" skipped over months of necessary mental preparation. You acted logically; he is reacting emotionally. When you are both operating on completely different wavelengths, demanding that he admit you were right will only make him dig his heels in further.

If you want to save this opportunity, you have to temporarily let go of being "right" about the miscommunication and focus on the shared reality: you have a life-changing offer on the table, and the clock is ticking. You can hold him accountable for his stonewalling while still extending the grace to acknowledge why he feels blindsided.

If you offer him a genuine bridge to talk and he still chooses to punish you by ignoring the deadline, what is your gut telling you to do about Denver?
